item.title: Marine outlet a boost to tourism
item.description: ASCO Motors has opened its new Yamaha outlet at Port Denarau in Nadi to provide a more accessible and efficient service for its customers. Acting sales and marketing manager Seiji Tokito said most of their customers are based at Port Denarau.
item.content:encoded:
ASCO Motors has opened its new Yamaha outlet at Port Denarau in Nadi to provide a more accessible and efficient service for its customers.

Acting sales and marketing manager Seiji Tokito said most of their customers are based at Port Denarau.

“We wanted to get closer to where our customers are so that we can provide that support for their business, for their outboards and servicing needs,” Mr Tokito said.

“We wanted to make sure that whenever we’re needed, we are right there at their doorstep.”

According to the company, Denarau was selected for its significance as a key gateway to Fiji’s tourism industry and home to one of the South Pacific’s busiest marinas.

Its central location offers Yamaha the opportunity to work more closely with customers and partners operating within the marine and tourism sectors.

The facility will serve as a hub for customer support, technical assistance, business development and stakeholder collaboration, allowing Yamaha to better support commercial operators, tourism businesses, marine transport providers, fishing enterprises, government agencies, and recreational users.

Speaking at the opening this week, Mr Tokito described the new addition as an important milestone for the growth of the Yamaha brand in Fiji.

“Our focus is not only on delivering world-class products but also on building long-term relationships based on trust, service, and shared success.

“The new office reflects our commitment to supporting our customers and contributing to the future growth of Fiji’s marine industry.”

Team Yamaha representative Vasiti Tanumi (third from left) along with Asco Motors staff at the opening of the Yamaha workshop at Port Denarau Marina, Nadi. Picture: BALJEET SINGH

item.title: Tech brain drain a potential gain
item.description: Government is brushing off concerns that providing tech start-ups access to overseas markets will trigger a brain drain, arguing that global exposure will ultimately benefit the domestic economy through remittances and diaspora investment. Addressing worries that international opportunities might encourage young entrepreneurs to relocate permanently, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Commerce
item.content:encoded:
Government is brushing off concerns that providing tech start-ups access to overseas markets will trigger a brain drain, arguing that global exposure will ultimately benefit the domestic economy through remittances and diaspora investment.

Addressing worries that international opportunities might encourage young entrepreneurs to relocate permanently, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Commerce and Business Development Manoa Kamikamica said local innovators remained tied to their roots regardless of where they operated.

He said a significant portion of present investments in Fiji originated from our citizens living abroad.

“The world is a global place now, so even if some of our tech innovators go offshore, they’ll still have Fijian blood in them,” Mr Kamikamica said.

“So, even if they’re offshore, what it means is they will be sending remittances back to their family.”

Central to this economic strategy is the newly launched Reserve Bank Innovation Hub, designed to foster local talent and diversify the economy into the ICT sector.

Mr Kamikamica drew comparisons to international successes like New Zealand’s accounting software giant Xero, which began as a start-up and evolved into a multi-billion-dollar global company.

“Just imagine one or two young men or women in Fiji owning a billion-dollar technological solution.

“It’s only a matter of time when Fiji will have its own Elon Musk or its own sort of Google founder as well.”

Mr Kamikamica said Government ministries were actively collaborating to help those young innovators scale up their operations.

Officials believe that while physical location may change, the financial and intellectual returns will continue flowing back to Fiji.

item.title: Denarau works ‘key to growth’
item.description: REGULAR planned maintenance works is key to economic progress, says Denarau Corporation Pte Ltd (DCL) general manager Nesbitt Hazelman. Responding to concerns raised about the recent wastewater leak along the Navakai to Denarau corridor in Nadi, Mr Hazelman said while these regular works were needed, utility providers were also constantly under pressure to service the public.
item.content:encoded:
REGULAR planned maintenance works is key to economic progress, says Denarau Corporation Pte Ltd (DCL) general manager Nesbitt Hazelman.

Responding to concerns raised about the recent wastewater leak along the Navakai to Denarau corridor in Nadi, Mr Hazelman said while these regular works were needed, utility providers were also constantly under pressure to service the public.

“… the current bust is off island, around 250 metres from the entry bridge on the swamp side,” he said.

“DCL continues to work closely with WAF, EFL and (Fiji) Roads Authority to ensure that stakeholders on the island are well informed of any disruptions that may be encountered during the repair works which has started (August 20) morning.

“We are of the view that infrastructure, whether it be new builds to support a particular area or regular planned repair and maintenance, is key to economic progress; it only helps support activity on the ground.

“We fully understand and appreciate the pressure that is exerted on the utility providers to provide uninterrupted services as they have their own unique challenges and priorities to deal with.”

Mr Hazelman said this was not the first time the reported leaks have happened and major stakeholders have been able to adjust and manage their operations.

“This is not the first event, and we all understand that it is an aging infrastructure and that Government has now committed funds to replace the current aging infrastructure.

“DCL currently manages and funds all infrastructure on the island while the utility providers are responsible for all infrastructure off the island; we have over the past few years developed a strong professional working relationship with our utility providers.”

item.title: New wave of co-ops
item.description: Fiji is taking a leading role in a regional cooperative movement across the Pacific Islands, aiming to expand the national economy through small business participation. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade Manoa Kamikamica highlighted the initiative emphasising the flexibility of the cooperative model in empowering various local demographics.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is taking a leading role in a regional cooperative movement across the Pacific Islands, aiming to expand the national economy through small business participation.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade Manoa Kamikamica highlighted the initiative emphasising the flexibility of the cooperative model in empowering various local demographics.

While traditional groups like farmers and taxi operators dominate the space, Mr Kamikamica said new sectors are emerging rapidly.

“The beauty about the cooperative model is it’s very flexible. So we are seeing a lot of women cooperatives, a lot of youth cooperatives, a lot of cooperatives with farmers,” he said.

Mr Kamikamica pointed to New Valley Farms in the Western Division, which currently houses about 20 established cooperatives with notable early success.

Although technology-focused cooperatives remain rare in Fiji, the minister expressed confidence that the country’s growing entrepreneurial spirit would soon change the landscape.

Mr Kamikamica said digital innovation was increasingly happening on a collaborative basis, with small teams joining forces to develop IT solutions.

“We haven’t seen many ICT-based cooperatives, but that is not saying that they won’t come.

“There’s now an emerging entrepreneurial spirit in Fiji that focuses very much on innovation and technology.”

Regional cooperation among Pacific Island nations is expected to generate broader economic activity, creating a stronger framework for small enterprises.

By expanding the reach of cooperatives beyond traditional sectors, Mr Kamikamica said the Fijian Government views this regional push as a vital milestone in diversifying the economy.

With support from government initiatives and collaborative set-ups, officials believe it is only a matter of time before tech-driven cooperatives become a staple of Fiji’s economic landscape.

item.title: Worry over drug use in young people
item.description: FIJI is facing a growing methamphetamine problem, with the drug increasingly affecting young people and communities, says Fiji Police Narcotics Division Inspector Usaia Donu. Mr Donu raised the concern during the 43rd Fiji Head Teachers Association’s annual conference in Nadi yesterday, where he called on teachers and educators to play a greater role in tackling substance misuse.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is facing a growing methamphetamine problem, with the drug increasingly affecting young people and communities, says Fiji Police Narcotics Division Inspector Usaia Donu.

Mr Donu raised the concern during the 43rd Fiji Head Teachers Association’s annual conference in Nadi yesterday, where he called on teachers and educators to play a greater role in tackling substance misuse.

He said drug use had become an increasing concern among young people, highlighting marijuana use and the number of teenagers who had received treatment for drug-related mental health conditions.

Mr Donu also referred to a major methamphetamine seizure in Legalega, Nadi, in early 2024, involving more than 4.2 tonnes of the drug.

He said more than 2400 drug-related cases had been recorded between 2024 and 2025, while marijuana cultivation and trafficking remained widespread in rural and maritime communities.

Mr Donu also raised concerns about drug use and HIV transmission, particularly through the sharing of needles.

He described methamphetamine, commonly known as ice or crystal meth, as an emerging threat and said the scale of the problem required urgent intervention.

“Fiji is no longer a transit hub, we are a domestic market now,” he said.

He urged schools, communities and law enforcement agencies to work together to protect young people and address the growing impact of drug abuse.

item.title: NZ travel agents seek urgent talks with Fiji over tourism tax
item.description: The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has arranged urgent talks with the Fijian Government over the implementation of the new five per cent Tourism Services Tax, warning Kiwi travellers with existing bookings could face unexpected additional costs. TAANZ says it is not opposing Fiji’s right to introduce the tax but wants bookings made before the September 1 commencement date to be exempt.
item.content:encoded:
The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has arranged urgent talks with the Fijian Government over the implementation of the new five per cent Tourism Services Tax, warning Kiwi travellers with existing bookings could face unexpected additional costs.

TAANZ says it is not opposing Fiji’s right to introduce the tax but wants bookings made before the September 1 commencement date to be exempt.

The new five per cent Tourism Services Tax will apply to tourism services, including hotels, restaurants and tour operators with annual turnover above $2 million. Revenue collected from the tax is to be ring-fenced to support Fiji Airways.

TAANZ chief executive officer Julie White said the association’s main concern was how the tax would affect holidays booked and, in many cases, fully paid for before the new tax was announced.

“Our concern is simple: travellers who booked and agreed a price before 1 September should not be hit with an additional tax simply because they are travelling after that date,” Ms White said.

“There is a significant volume of existing Fiji bookings where the price has already been agreed, and in many cases the customer has paid in full.”

She said those travellers had a reasonable expectation their holidays had already been paid for and should not suddenly face another cost.

The timing is also concerning for the New Zealand travel industry because the tax takes effect immediately before the busy September and October school holiday period.

“Families have planned and budgeted for these holidays months in advance,” Ms White said.

She said group, wedding and corporate bookings could also be affected where contracts and prices had already been finalised.

TAANZ also wants clarification on who is responsible for collecting the tax, its treatment of net rates and existing contracts, and the division of responsibilities between suppliers and travel agents.

The association wants the tax to apply according to when a booking or purchase was made rather than when the travel takes place.

“Grandfathering existing bookings is the fairest outcome,” Ms White said.

“It protects travellers who purchased in good faith, gives the travel industry certainty and allows the new tax to be implemented cleanly for new bookings from 1 September.”

TAANZ said more than 219,000 New Zealanders visited Fiji in 2025, accounting for 22.2 per cent of visitor arrivals and making New Zealand Fiji’s second-largest visitor market behind Australia.

Ms White said providing certainty would help maintain Kiwi confidence in Fiji as a destination.

TAANZ is working alongside the Australian Travel Industry Association, which has raised similar concerns.

The two organisations are expected to meet with the Fijian Government ahead of the September 1 implementation date to seek clarity and raise concerns over existing bookings.

item.title: Australian travel industry hits out at Fiji tourism tax rollout
item.description: Australia’s peak travel industry body has criticised the rollout of Fiji’s new five per cent tourism tax, warning its application to existing bookings could leave travellers facing unexpected additional costs. The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) says the tax, which takes effect from September 1, should not be retrospectively applied to holidays already booked and paid for.
item.content:encoded:
Australia’s peak travel industry body has criticised the rollout of Fiji’s new five per cent tourism tax, warning its application to existing bookings could leave travellers facing unexpected additional costs.

The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) says the tax, which takes effect from September 1, should not be retrospectively applied to holidays already booked and paid for.

“The design and rollout reflect a complete lack of understanding of how the travel booking ecosystem works, and it is travellers and travel businesses who will pay the price for that failure,” ATIA chief executive officer Dean Long said.

“Retrospective application is an absolute no-go. Once a customer has paid, that price is locked in.”

Mr Long said asking customers to pay additional charges after completing their bookings amounted to “a broken promise dressed up as policy”.

He said travellers were now being asked to find additional money for holidays they believed had been fully paid for months earlier.

“That is not how you treat people who chose Fiji in good faith,” he said.

ATIA has also criticised what it says was a lack of consultation with the Australian and New Zealand travel industries before the tax changes were announced.

“None of this needed to happen. The tax arrived with zero consultation with the travel industry in Australia or New Zealand despite the significant importance of these markets to Fiji,” Mr Long said.

He said Australia was Fiji’s largest tourism market and New Zealand its second-largest, yet the industry was given just over two weeks between the announcement and implementation of the tax.

Mr Long said this provided insufficient time for businesses to update contracts and pricing systems or properly advise travellers.

The Travel Agents’ Association of New Zealand has raised similar concerns and is calling for existing bookings to be exempt from the new tax.

“Grandfathering existing bookings is the fairest outcome,” TAANZ chief executive officer Julie White said.

“It protects travellers who purchased in good faith, gives the travel industry certainty and allows the new tax to be implemented cleanly for new bookings from 1 September.”

From September 1, the five per cent tax is set to apply to tourism operators, including hotel, tourism and cruise businesses, with annual turnover above $2 million .

The measure forms part of taxation changes announced under Fiji’s 2026-2027 National Budget.

item.title: Bill proposes 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council
item.description: A 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council comprising government and private sector representatives would be established under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 tabled in Parliament yesterday. The proposed legislation establishes the Fiji Yaqona Council as a corporate body with powers to oversee its affairs, own and dispose of property, enter into contracts, appoint agents and engage consultants.
item.content:encoded:
A 16-member Fiji Yaqona Council comprising government and private sector representatives would be established under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026 tabled in Parliament yesterday.

The proposed legislation establishes the Fiji Yaqona Council as a corporate body with powers to oversee its affairs, own and dispose of property, enter into contracts, appoint agents and engage consultants.

Under the Bill, the Council would consist of eight ex-officio government members and eight representatives from the private sector, all appointed by the Minister.

The Permanent Secretary would serve as chairperson of the Council.

Other government representatives would include officials responsible for commerce, health, rural and maritime development, foreign affairs and iTaukei affairs.

The Chief Executive Officer of the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji, or a representative, would also sit on the Council.

Private sector representation would comprise four members nominated by the Yaqona Working Group and four additional yaqona operators.

The relevant sectors or bodies would nominate their representatives, with the Minister appointing members from among those nominated.

Private sector members would be appointed for terms of up to three years and would be eligible for reappointment.

However, they would not be permitted to serve for more than six consecutive years.

Ex-officio members would remain on the Council for as long as they held the government position through which they were appointed.

Members would also be able to resign by providing the Minister with at least 30 days’ written notice.

The proposed Council would have the legal capacity to sue and be sued, purchase and hold property, sell or lease property and enter into contracts.

It would also be able to appoint agents and attorneys, engage consultants and set charges and other terms for services and facilities it provides.

The Council would have its own common seal, with documents requiring the seal to be signed by the Chief Executive or another duly authorised person.

The establishment of the Council forms part of the broader regulatory framework proposed under the Yaqona (Kava) Bill 2026.
